How do objects get charged by rubbing?
questions.a: Rubbing transfers electrons from one body to the other, giving both equal but opposite charges.

questions.q: Name the charge left on a glass rod rubbed with silk.
questions.a: Positive - the rod loses electrons to the silk, which becomes negative.

questions.q: Is charging by rubbing a chemical change?
questions.a: No - only electrons move; no new substance forms.

concepts.title: Types of Charges and Their Interaction

questions.q: What two kinds of charges exist in nature?
questions.a: Positive and negative charges.

questions.q: State the rule of attraction and repulsion between charges.
questions.a: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

questions.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall. What does that show?
questions.a: The charged balloon induces opposite charge on the wall's surface, and unlike charges attract.

questions.q: How can we detect charge on a body?
questions.a: With an electroscope - a charge on its plate makes the aluminium leaves spread apart.

questions.q: How does charge transfer happen between two bodies?
questions.a: By touching - electrons flow from the body with excess electrons to one with fewer till both share equally.

questions.q: What happens to an electroscope when a charged rod touches it?
questions.a: The leaves get the same charge and repel each other, standing apart; they fold back when discharged.

questions.q: What is earthing?
questions.a: Connecting a body to the earth with a metal wire so extra charge flows safely into the ground.

questions.q: Why are tall buildings and appliances earthed?
questions.a: Earthing gives leaking charge an easy path to the ground, protecting people from shocks.

questions.q: How does charge get discharged from a charged body?
questions.a: A spark or flow of charge passes when the body touches something at a different potential, often through air.

questions.q: What is lightning?
questions.a: A giant electric spark between clouds, or between clouds and the earth, as huge charges discharge.

questions.q: How do clouds collect charge?
questions.a: Rubbing of water drops and ice inside clouds separates charges - tops turn positive, bottoms negative.

questions.q: Why does lightning often strike tall trees and buildings?
questions.a: Tall objects give charge the shortest path to the ground, so the spark prefers them.

questions.q: What is a lightning conductor?
questions.a: A pointed metal rod on a building joined by a thick wire to the ground, which carries lightning charge safely down.

questions.q: Where should you shelter during lightning outdoors?
questions.a: Inside a building or car; never under a lone tall tree or in open water.

questions.q: Name two lightning safety rules indoors.
questions.a: Avoid wired phones and electrical appliances; keep away from windows, taps and metal pipes.

questions.q: What causes an earthquake?
questions.a: Sudden movements of the tectonic plates of the earth's crust release built-up strain as tremors.

questions.q: What is the place inside the earth where a quake begins called?
questions.a: The focus; the point above it on the surface is the epicentre.

questions.q: Name two natural and one human cause of earthquakes.
questions.a: Natural: moving tectonic plates, volcanoes. Human: mining and big dams can trigger tremors.

questions.q: What is a seismograph?
questions.a: An instrument that records the tremors (seismic waves) of an earthquake on a paper or screen record.

questions.q: What is the Richter scale used for?
questions.a: Rating the energy of an earthquake in numbers - each higher number means much stronger shaking.

questions.q: Can scientists predict earthquakes reliably?
questions.a: No - they can locate and measure past quakes, but prediction of time and place is still not possible.

questions.q: How should you protect yourself during an earthquake indoors?
questions.a: Take cover under a strong table against an inside wall, keep away from windows and heavy furniture, and stay calm.

questions.q: What should you do outdoors when an earthquake strikes?
questions.a: Move to open ground away from buildings, trees, poles and power lines.

questions.q: Name two preparations that make a house earthquake-safe.
questions.a: Fix cupboards and heavy objects to walls, and build with quake-resistant designs following safety codes.
